works, because it never depended on the agent in the first place.

Gate is a *consumer* of the `entire graph` provider, and the graph was also the primary
navigation tool while building it:

- `entire graph snapshot` — symbols, relations and file records feed `collect`.
- `entire graph diff` / `checkpoint` — the entity-level semantic diff Gate ranks.
- `entire graph capabilities` — feature-detection before trusting semantic relations

## 1. The story — what is "Gate"?

Imagine you asked a super-fast robot to fix your homework. The robot comes back and says:

> "Done! I changed 47 pages."

You now have a horrible problem. Reading all 47 pages is *more work than doing the homework yourself*, which defeats the whole point of having a robot. But if you just say "looks good!" without reading, you might hand in something broken.

**Gate is the third choice.** You run one command:

```sh
./entire-graph gate --repo . --base HEAD~3 --head HEAD
```

and it tells you three things:

1. **Which 4 of the 47 pages you actually need to read** (a ranked list — most dangerous first)
2. **What nobody checked** — pieces the robot changed that no test looks at
3. **A verdict**: `keep` ✅ / `continue` 🟡 / `revert` ❌ — and a matching exit code (0/1/2), so it can even block a `git push`

## 2. The clever bit — Gate never asks the robot anything

Most review tools read the robot's own description of what it did. That's like asking the kid who broke the vase whether the vase is broken.

Gate refuses to read the description. Instead it only looks at things the robot **could not have made up**:

| Evidence | Where it comes from | Why the robot can't fake it |
|---|---|---|
| **Blast radius** — what else breaks | the code graph: who *calls* this function | those callers were written months ago by other people |
| **Coverage** — who checked it | the project's own test files | a test either exists or it doesn't |

And the second half of the idea: **Gate reports absence.** Other tools tell you what they found. Gate tells you what *nobody looked at*. "Unchecked" gets its own count and is never quietly mixed into "verified" — because a gate with no test is not a gate that passed.

Think of a kitchen. Only **one** room is allowed to get messy (touch the disk, git, the outside world). Everything else is clean and easy to test.

| Layer | File | Job | Messy? |

| collect | [internal/cli/gate.go](internal/cli/gate.go) | goes out and fetches the diff + the graph | **yes** — the only one |
| index | [internal/gate/index.go](internal/gate/index.go) | builds the "who points at who" map | no |
| signals | [risk.go](internal/gate/risk.go), [coverage.go](internal/gate/coverage.go) | counts dependents; finds tests | no |
| verdict | [verdict.go](internal/gate/verdict.go) | turns findings → keep/continue/revert | no |
| render | [render.go](internal/gate/render.go) | prints it (text or `--json`) | no |
| contract | [types.go](internal/gate/types.go) | the shared shapes | no |

# Part 1 — The story (ELI10)

## The problem

You ask a robot to fix your homework. It comes back: **"Done! I changed 47 pages."**

Now you're stuck:
- **Read all 47 pages** → more work than doing the homework yourself. The robot was pointless.
- **Say "looks good!"** → this is how broken homework gets handed in.

Git can tell you *which lines* changed. It cannot tell you what those lines can **break**, which of them anyone **checked**, or which forty-eighth page everybody **forgot**.

## Gate is the third choice

One command:

```sh
entire graph gate --repo . --base HEAD~3 --head HEAD
```

You get back:

1. **A ranked reading order** — "of your 583 changed things, read these 5 first"
2. **What nobody checked** — "306 unchecked"
3. **A verdict + exit code** — `keep`(0) / `continue`(1) / `revert`(2) / `unusable`(5), so it can literally block a `git push`

## The trick nobody else does: never ask the robot

Most review tools read the robot's commit message. That's asking the kid who broke the vase whether the vase is broken.

**Gate refuses to read the description.** It only looks at things the robot could not have invented:

| Question | Where the answer comes from | Can the robot fake it? |
|---|---|---|
| *What breaks?* | the code graph — who **calls** this | No. Those callers were written months ago by other people. |
| *Who checked it?* | the repo's own test files | No. A test file either exists and points here, or it doesn't. |

## And the second trick: it reports **absence**

Every other tool tells you what it **found**. Gate tells you what **nobody looked at**.

`unchecked` gets its own number and is *never* quietly added to "verified". **A gate with no test is not a gate that passed.**

---

# Part 2 — High level: the pipeline

One messy room, five clean ones. Only one layer is allowed to touch the outside world.

```
  --checkpoint <id>   |   --base <ref> --head <ref>
                    │
                    ▼
     ┌──────────────────────────┐
     │  COLLECT  (impure)       │  internal/cli/gate.go
     │  git diff + build graph  │  the ONLY layer that reads disk/git
     └────────────┬─────────────┘
                  ▼
     ┌──────────────────────────┐
     │  INDEX                   │  index.go — flip every "A calls B" arrow
     │  who-depends-on-me map   │  around, so "who breaks?" is one lookup
     └────────────┬─────────────┘
          ┌───────┴────────┐
          ▼                ▼
     ┌─────────┐      ┌──────────┐
     │  RISK   │      │ COVERAGE │   pure. no disk, no git, no compiler.
     │ how many│      │ any test │
     │ callers?│      │ reach it?│
     └────┬────┘      └────┬─────┘
          └───────┬────────┘
                  ▼
          ┌───────────────┐
          │   VERDICT     │  verdict.go — findings → keep/continue/revert
          └───────┬───────┘
                  ▼
          ┌───────────────┐
          │    RENDER     │  render.go — text or --json
          └───────────────┘
```

**Why the split matters:** `internal/gate` deliberately does **not** import `internal/sem`. Importing it would drag in tree-sitter and C compilation. So all 50 tests run in **0.44 seconds** with no git, no repo, no C compiler. That's the architectural bet, and it paid off.

---

# Part 3 — Low level: what each piece actually does

## 3.1 collect — [internal/cli/gate.go](internal/cli/gate.go)

```go
result   := sem.AnalyzeGitRange(...)       // or AnalyzeCheckpoint(id)
snapshot := sem.BuildProviderSnapshotWithOptions(ctx, repo, version,
                sem.ProfileFull)           // full, NOT fast — see below
index    := gate.NewIndex(projectSymbols(snapshot), projectRelations(snapshot))
markPartialAnalysis(index, snapshot)
```

Four details worth knowing:

- **`ProfileFull` is required, not preferred.** `fast` omits `USES_TYPE`, `PARAM_TYPE`, `RETURNS_TYPE` — three of the twelve edge types the blast radius walks. Cost: ~23s wall / 57s CPU on this repo.
- **If the graph fails to build, Gate does not accuse anybody.** It records a warning and lets the verdict degrade to `unusable` (exit 5).
- **`verifyCommand` uses an ordered slice, not a map** — Go randomises map iteration, and a tool whose pitch is "run it twice, get the same bytes" cannot afford that.
- **`changedEntities` sorts by (path, name, line)** rather than trusting git's ordering.

## 3.2 index — [internal/gate/index.go](internal/gate/index.go)

Builds `incoming[symbolID] → []dependencyEdge`. Twelve edge types count as dependencies:

```
CALLS  ASYNC_CALLS  CONSTRUCTS  USES_TYPE  PARAM_TYPE  RETURNS_TYPE
READS_FIELD  WRITES_FIELD  EXTENDS  IMPLEMENTS  OVERRIDES  INHERITS
```

**Three are deliberately excluded**, and one of those exclusions is the best bug story in the project:

- `CONTAINS` / `DEFINES` — structural, not behavioural. A file containing a symbol isn't a caller of it.
- **`DATA_FLOWS`** — this one *looks* right and is exactly backwards. The provider emits `resolveRepo -> runStats` with reason *"callee return value assigned to local and returned by caller"* — that's the **callee pointing at its caller**. Reversed for a "who depends on me" walk, it reads as the precise inverse of the truth. Removing it took `runStats` from **156 → 130** dependents. The lesson generalises: **an edge type's direction is not automatically its dependency direction — read the `reason` field first.**

Then `DependentsWithTier` does a bounded BFS (`hops ≤ 2`), sorts by (path, name, ID), and dedupes by location — because one symbol can be reached through two `compound-v1` IDs and would otherwise be counted and printed twice.

## 3.3 risk — [internal/gate/risk.go](internal/gate/risk.go)

Only **breaking** changes open a finding:

```go
func (c ChangeType) Breaking() bool {
    return c == Removed || c == Renamed || c == SignatureChanged
}
```

A `body_changed` with 100 callers is **not** a risk finding — its signature still holds, so callers still compile and still mean what they meant. Reporting it would bury the changes that can actually break someone.

## 3.4 coverage — [internal/gate/coverage.go](internal/gate/coverage.go)

Three states, and the third is the whole point:

- `verified` — a test file has an incoming edge to this symbol
- `unchecked` — the resolver ran and found nothing
- `no-resolver` — **we couldn't look here at all**

Reporting `no-resolver` as `unchecked` would be charging the author for Gate's own blind spot. It's read off the graph rather than by running a search per entity — a search probe would be more thorough and cost seconds each, which on 583 entities is minutes.

## 3.5 verdict — [internal/gate/verdict.go](internal/gate/verdict.go)

```
revert   = breaking change · ≥1 PROVEN dependent · no covering test
continue = breaking change with dependents, OR anything unchecked,
           OR anything in a region the graph couldn't see
keep     = none of the above
unusable = no dimension produced evidence
```

Two invariants that never bend:

> **DEGRADATION** — a dimension that did not run cannot produce a finding against you.
> **EVIDENCE** — only *confirmed* structural evidence may accuse.

The first one is subtle and load-bearing: `revert` reads "has dependents **AND** no covering test". If coverage never ran, then *nothing* has a covering test, and every dependent-bearing change would read as `revert` — a false accusation manufactured by a **missing input**.

## 3.6 The curveball layer — [internal/gate/evidence.go](internal/gate/evidence.go)

The 12:00 constraint: *"static analysis can't fully resolve dynamic dispatch / generated code / reflection. Don't present incomplete relationships as certain."*

**Why it hurt (ELI10):** Gate was drawing a map and printing **"0 houses on this street."** Sometimes the truth was **"it was too foggy to see that street."** Those are completely different sentences — and "0 dependents" is *exactly* the condition where Gate stays quiet and says `keep`.

**Gate was most confident precisely where the graph was blindest.** For a tool whose entire pitch is "we report what nobody checked," that's the worst possible failure.

The root cause was **one line**. The provider already told the truth — every relation carries `Confidence` and `Resolution`. Gate threw it all away at the projection boundary:

```go
gate.Relation{FromID: r.FromID, ToID: r.ToID, Type: r.Type}   // confidence: dropped
```

Three tiers now:

| Tier | Meaning | Prints as | Can it accuse? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `confirmed` | the graph **proved** it | `8 dependents` | ✅ may reach `revert` |
| `heuristic` `~` | the graph **guessed** it | `~130 dependents (none proven)` | ❌ caps at `continue` |
| `unresolvable` `?` | the graph **couldn't look** | `dependents unresolvable (graph could not see this region)` | ❌ caps at `continue`, **always reported** |

Keyed on the provider's **resolution method**, measured not guessed ([curveball-resolution-distribution.txt](docs/graph-findings/curveball-resolution-distribution.txt)):

```
31487 exact           ─┐ confirmed
  738 import_resolved ─┘
 8217 import_external ─┐
 7190 package          │
 5186 name_only        ├ heuristic — a match by name/shape/package,
 4230 pattern          │ any of which can point at the wrong symbol
 2552 type_inferred    │
   57 git_history     ─┘
```

**The calibration story is the best comment in the codebase.** The first attempt used `confidence >= 0.9`. But real `"exact"` edges carry confidences of 1, 0.92, 0.85 **and** 0.7 — so that threshold demoted **6,737 genuinely exact edges** and made nearly everything print as uncertain:

> *"A tool that marks everything uncertain has not become more honest — it has just moved the noise, and a reader learns to ignore the marker."*

---

# Part 4 — What makes you stand out

1. **You never ask the subject.** Every other agent-review tool reads the agent's own summary. Gate structurally *cannot* — there's no code path that reads a commit message. An agent cannot talk its way to `keep`.
2. **You report absence, not presence.** `unchecked` is a first-class number. Nobody else prints "here's what nobody looked at."
3. **Two-way honesty about uncertainty.** Most tools that add confidence scores only guard against *over*-claiming. Gate's curveball fix caught the *under*-claim — "0 dependents" hiding a blind spot — which is the one that actually ships bugs.
4. **The verdict is a printed rule, not a black box.** `Rule` is emitted with every single run. A reviewer who disagrees can read the rule without reading the source.
5. **It found real bugs in itself and in upstream, and disclosed them instead of hiding them.** The `DATA_FLOWS` inversion, two determinism bugs, a nondeterminism in `internal/sem`. §8 of [BUILDATHON.md](BUILDATHON.md) lists limitations judges would otherwise have to find.
6. **Purity as a design constraint, not a slogan.** 50 tests / 0.44s / no CGO, because one boundary was drawn correctly on day one. The curveball landed as *one new file plus a struct field* — that's the architecture paying rent.

---

# Part 5 — Edge cases & optimisations (found by running it, just now)

I built the binary and ran `gate --base HEAD~3 --head HEAD`. **Exit 2, `revert`, 23.5s.** Here's what the real output exposes, ranked by how much it hurts a judge's read.

### 🔴 P0-1 — Markdown headings are being reported as changed code entities

```
583 entities changed
```

But of the 204 `added` entities marked unresolvable:

```
  section 1.-One-sentence           @ PLAN.md
  section 12.-The-Noon-Curveball…   @ PLAN.md
  code_fence                        @ PLAN.md
  → 64 entities from PLAN.md alone; kinds: section(48), code_fence(16)
```

Gate is analysing the blast radius of **its own documentation headings** and then reporting "the graph could not resolve dependents" for them. This inflates `583 entities`, inflates `259 unresolvable`, and makes the PARTIAL ANALYSIS banner look far scarier than reality. **Fix:** filter non-code kinds out of the change set in `changedEntities`, or exclude them from the risk/coverage dimensions.

### 🔴 P0-2 — The "files analysis could not complete" list is 95% noise

```
files analysis could not complete:
  - .claude-plugin/marketplace.json (JSON is inventory-only…)
  - .claude/agents/entire-search.md (Markdown is inventory-only…)
  - .entire/.gitignore (Git Ignore is inventory-only…)
  ... and 86 more
```

**94 partial paths. Exactly 5 are code files** (the C# grammar `array.h` parse failures — the ones that actually matter). A `.gitignore` cannot hide a caller. The real signal is buried under 89 lines of config files. **Fix:** don't mark data/doc-only languages partial, or split the section into "failed to parse" (real) vs "not analysed" (expected).

### 🔴 P0-3 — Coverage findings falsely render as `[confirmed]`

```
changedEntities @ internal/cli/gate.go:205   [confirmed]
    function added is unchecked: no test covers it (2 dependents)
```

`Coverage()` never sets `Finding.Tier`, so the zero value falls through `tierLabel` to `"confirmed"`. Worse conceptually: **coverage is graph-derived too**. "No test covers it" in a region the graph couldn't see is *not* a confirmed claim — it's the exact same under-claim the curveball was about, just in the other dimension. The curveball fixed `risk` and missed `coverage`.

### 🟠 P1-1 — Tier propagation makes proven dependents vanish

```
Run @ internal/cli/root.go:43
    body_changed · 232 dependents (2 proven, 230 inferred)
```

Only **2 of 232** proven. In `DependentsWithTier`, a dependent's tier is set by the **first** path that reaches it (BFS order = sorted adjacency = alphabetical). One heuristic edge early in the walk poisons everything behind it. But **existence of one proven path proves the dependency** — the tier should be the *best* path, not the first. Fix is a best-first walk (expand confirmed edges to fixpoint first, then heuristic). This would likely turn `2 proven` into something genuinely useful, and it directly affects the `revert` rule.

### 🟠 P1-2 — Removed and renamed entities can never trigger `revert`

```
removed:  27 unresolvable / 1 confirmed     (28 total)
renamed:  19 unresolvable / 0 confirmed     (19 total)
```

**100% of renames and 96% of removals resolve to nothing.** Cause: Gate builds *one* snapshot, of `HEAD`. A removed symbol is by definition **absent from HEAD**, so `ix.Resolve` returns zero IDs → `Unresolvable` → `Proven()` false → can never reach `revert`. Removal is the *most* breaking change type there is, and it's the one Gate is structurally blind to. Correct fix is a base-side snapshot for removed/renamed entities; the honest short-term fix is to say so in §8.

### 🟡 P2 — Optimisations

| # | Issue | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| a | `ResolveCoverage` re-walks hop-1 dependents that `Risk` already computed for every entity | share the hop-1 result |
| b | `ix.Resolve(name, path)` runs twice per entity (risk + coverage) | resolve once, cache on the entity |
| c | `Coverage()` truncates to 10 by **alphabetical** order, not most-dependents-first | sort `withDependents` by `e.Dependents` desc before the cap |
| d | 23.5s wall / 57s CPU, every run, no cache | `entire graph index --head --profile full` warm-up; document it |
| e | `snapshotHasTests(snapshot)` called twice | hoist |

### ⚪ Also noted

- `Proven()` returns false whenever `Region == Unresolvable` — so a change with genuinely proven dependents *in a partially-analysed file* is downgraded. Arguably backwards: a blind spot means the risk is **larger**, not smaller. Worth a deliberate decision either way.
- [BUILDATHON.md](BUILDATHON.md) still says **"27 tests, 78.9%"** in §4 and §8. Reality is **50 tests, 72.0%**. §6's "Built · not built" doesn't mention evidence tiers at all.
- `W_MOVE_AMBIGUOUS internal/cli/stats.go` — moves reported as remove/add, which is part of why 583 entities.

---

Before I start editing: P0-1/2/3 are unambiguous bugs and I'd fix those regardless. P1-1 and P1-2 change what verdict Gate produces, which is a real call to make this close to a submission.

Third bucket landed on my side — you need one change: stamp gate.RuntimeDispatchPrefix on the reason string when you MarkPartial for reflection. No Index API change needed.

I went with a variant of your (b), but not string-sniffing: an exported tag constant, which is the pattern NotAnalysedPrefix already established and which you accepted. Reason I did not take (a): changing MarkPartial's signature ripples through every caller and probably Analysis too, and we are close enough to the deadline that I would rather not have a cross-lane signature change in flight. If you still prefer the typed field afterwards it is a clean refactor later.

WHAT YOU DO — in index.go/risk.go wherever you mark a reflection finding partial:
  index.MarkPartial(path, gate.RuntimeDispatchPrefix+" "+reason)
(inside the package it is just RuntimeDispatchPrefix). Keep the reason text exactly as it is; I strip the tag before printing, so the reader sees what they see today.

WHAT I DID — render.go only:
  const RuntimeDispatchPrefix = "runtime dispatch:"
  writeAnalysis now buckets into three groups, in this order:
    parsed fine, but callers may be resolved at runtime (N)
    failed to parse (N)
    never analysed for relations (N)
Runtime dispatch leads deliberately. A parse failure says the graph could not read the code; an inventory-only file says it never tried; runtime dispatch says it read everything, understood it, and the answer is still incomplete. That last one is the curveball stated exactly, and it was the one buried.

It degrades gracefully: until you stamp the tag, reflection files keep appearing under "failed to parse" exactly as now. Nothing breaks in between.

INDEPENDENT CONFIRMATION OF YOUR BUG, at larger scale. I cloned django (7087 files, 75M) and ran Gate: 30.5s, exit 1, 81 entities. Found them, and testing on real repos immediately paid for itself — it exposed two bugs, one of them mine.

## The five repos, chosen so each breaks static analysis a *different* way

| Repo | Lang | Files | Gate time | Dispatch mechanism |

| **nestjs/nest** | TS | 2,307 | 12.9s | decorator DI via `reflect-metadata` |
| **django** | Python | **7,087** | **30.5s** | import-by-string, metaclasses, signals |

All five ran clean — exit 1, no crash, no timeout. Saved to [docs/graph-findings/cross-repo-test-matrix.txt](docs/graph-findings/cross-repo-test-matrix.txt).

**Django is your headline.** 7,087 files in 30s, and it's the framework whose entire plugin model is import-by-string:

```
?qualname @ django/utils/module_loading.py:124
  dependents could not be resolved (Python dynamic import is imported here)
  — the 44 shown is a floor, not a count
```

44 dependents reported as a *floor*, in the module-loading file. That's a stronger demo beat than flask.

**gin is your best single counter-example.** `Engine.ServeHTTP` — the function every request in the framework passes through — resolves to **exactly one caller: a benchmark, at resolution `type_inferred`**. Every production caller goes through `http.Handler` and leaves no edge. That's the interface-dispatch gap made concrete, now in §8 with the measurement.

## Two bugs the real repos found

**Mine.** Entity kind `document` (the whole-file entity for a `.rst`) wasn't in `proseKinds` — 3 in pytest, 6 in scrapy. One of them, `doc/en/reference/plugin_list.rst`, matched a `HANDLES_TOOL` edge and got reported as *"registered as a tool handler: its callers are external invocations."* A reStructuredText page described as a live entry point. Fixed with a regression test.

**b7's, which I confirmed at 50× their scale.** They saw 2 mislabelled files on flask. Django showed **99** files under "failed to parse" that had parsed perfectly — they were reflection-flagged. Same channel, wrong bucket.

I fixed the render side with a third group, ordered by what each actually claims:

```
parsed fine, but callers may be resolved at runtime (N)   ← the curveball, stated exactly
failed to parse (N)
never analysed for relations (N)
```

Runtime dispatch leads deliberately: a parse failure means the graph couldn't *read* the code; runtime dispatch means it read everything, understood it, and the answer is *still* incomplete. That was the strongest evidence Gate produces and it was buried under a false label. b7 needs a one-line change to stamp the tag — it degrades gracefully until they do.

Also added to §8: languages whose dispatch is a builtin (JS `eval`, Ruby `send`, PHP variable functions) import nothing, so there's no `IMPORTS` edge to key on and Gate reports a confident zero.

## Verification

```

go test ./internal/gate/ -cover    58 tests, 84.4%
go test ./...                      all packages ok
```

Risk's not-in-graph branch fires for every entity Resolve misses, and a removed entity is ALWAYS missing from the head snapshot — the snapshot is of HEAD and the thing was removed. So "X is not in the graph: no dependent analysis was possible here" is a tautology for change_type=removed. All five are real source changes in rewrite.py. So ranking is fine; only the findings section is wrong.

1. Do not emit a per-entity risk finding when change_type is removed or renamed. Keep everything else exactly as now: still tier the entity Unresolvable, still count it in Analysis, still let it force continue via Decide's unresolvable arm, still show it in the review order. It just stops spending a findings slot on a tautology.

3. If you want to keep per-entity findings, then at minimum sort source removals above test-file removals — gate.IsTestPath is already exported from coverage.go and is the same predicate coverage uses.

Two different questions in "did u run tests" — let me separate them.

## What I ran

**Yes** — Gate itself, on all five, and just now re-run on a **single final binary** so the numbers are consistent (the first table mixed three builds as I fixed things):

| Repo | Files | Time | Verdict | Runtime-dispatch files detected |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| gin | 130 | 2.1s | `keep` | 13 (Go `reflect` in `binding/`) |
| scrapy | 680 | 5.5s | `continue` | 27 (`importlib`/`inspect`/`pkgutil`) |
| pytest | 690 | 9.6s | `continue` | pluggy hooks |
| nest | 2,307 | 12.0s | `continue` | decorator DI |
| django | **7,087** | 30.6s | `continue` | **96** (import-by-string, metaclasses) |

**No** — I did *not* run those projects' own test suites (django's, pytest's). That would prove nothing about Gate and takes far longer than the time we have.

## Bugs fixed

Your five repos found three defects our own repo never could:

**1. `document` kind escaped the prose filter** (pytest, scrapy). `doc/en/reference/plugin_list.rst` matched a `HANDLES_TOOL` edge and got reported as *"registered as a tool handler: its callers are external invocations."* A docs page described as a live HTTP entry point.

**2. 96 Django files printed under "failed to parse" — none had failed.** They were reflection-flagged, sharing the Index's partial channel with real parse errors. Runtime dispatch now has its own bucket and **leads** the listing:

```
parsed fine, but callers may be resolved at runtime (96)
failed to parse (0)
never analysed for relations (115)
```

That ordering matters — it's the one claim only this tool makes, and it was buried under a false label.

**3. gin: 9 GitHub Actions jobs reported `unchecked` at tier `confirmed`.** Gate asserting with full confidence that `jobs.trivy-scan` has no unit test. True, and a category error — nobody was ever going to unit-test a release job. Coverage now returns `NoResolver` for CI/CD kinds. They stay in the change set and risk still ranks them; a broken release job is a real defect, just not a coverage one.

## ⚠️ One consequence you should veto if you disagree

Fix 3 moved **gin from `continue` (exit 1) to `keep` (exit 0)**. That's a real softening. It's honest — the header now reads `1 verified · 0 unchecked · 9 no-resolver`, and every one of those 9 is a CI job — but it means a change set of nothing but CI edits can now pass. Say the word and I'll make pipeline entities cap at `continue` instead.
